terms.definition: Entering a building or part of a building as a trespasser with intent to steal, inflict grievous bodily harm or do unlawful damage.
terms.examiner: The intent must exist at the moment of entry. State which subsection applies before applying it.

terms.definition: Having entered a building or part of a building as a trespasser, stealing or attempting to steal, or inflicting or attempting to inflict grievous bodily harm.
terms.examiner: No intent is needed on entry; what matters is the offence committed inside.

terms.definition: Entry need only be effective, and it can be partial.
terms.examiner: R v Collins (substantial and effective), R v Brown (effective), R v Ryan (partial entry, head and arm through a window, was enough).

terms.definition: A person who enters without permission, or who goes beyond the permission given, knowing it or being reckless about it.
terms.examiner: R v Jones and Smith: going beyond the purpose of permission makes the entrant a trespasser. R v Walkington: part of a building, such as behind a counter.

terms.definition: A structure with some permanence; s9(4) includes inhabited vehicles and vessels.
terms.examiner: B and S v Leathley (a freezer container) and Norfolk Constabulary v Seekings (lorry trailers used for storage) show where the line falls.

terms.definition: Burglary committed while carrying a firearm, imitation firearm, weapon of offence or explosive.
terms.examiner: The weapon must be with the defendant at the time of the burglary (R v O'Leary); the maximum sentence is life imprisonment.
